content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes to pre-train on chemical reactions in order to learn a molecule representation that can be used for downstream tasks. The authors build on the MolR work, improving it by using yields to define an adaptive margin in the loss, and also adding a distillation component. Through experiments on reaction product ranking and property prediction, the authors show their MolKD works better than MolR and other baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
=== Strengths === 

(S1): This work addresses an important problem of learning molecule representations in an unsupervised way. The paper is clear and well-written. 

(S2): While it's a relatively small increment on top of MolR, the differences are clearly explained, and the performance differences looks statistically significant. There are good ablations showing that using yields is indeed responsible for the better performance. In particular, the MolKD-random and MolKD-confidence ablations are convincing. 

 

=== Weaknesses === 

(W1): It would be good to provide more intuition for why the distillation step is better than just directly using the teacher model and fine-tuning it: 

- While I appreciate that the authors provide a MolKD- ablation where the teacher model is used directly, it's not clear to me if the model is frozen, and if it's fine-tuned, whether the authors applied simple tweaks to make sure the fine-tuning works well (e.g. using a different learning rate for the backbone and a different one for the head). 

- I saw in the Appendix that the student model is actually smaller than the teacher model. Is that one of the reasons to introduce distillation here, to be able to use a smaller model for the downstream task? 

- If using distillation improves results even if the teacher and student models have the same architecture, could that be due to self-distillation effects? 

(W2): Conceptually, the method is a relatively small increment on top of MolR (although the authors did not try to hide that). 

 

=== Other comments === 

(O1): The authors mention that the set of atoms between the reactants and the products is always the same. This is only true if the reactions are fully reported, i.e. insignificant side products are not omitted. Patents often omit side products. Do all of the reactions in the dataset used here report all products, and are thus fully atom-mapped? I was confused about this, because at another point the authors mention that there is always exactly one product. Is this due to some aggressive filtering that was applied on top of the original patent data?

 

=== Nitpicks === 

Here I include some final nitpicks, which did not affect my score; they are here just to help improve the paper. 

- "Effective molecular representations plays" - both singular and plural at the same time 

- "model compressing" - maybe "model compression" 

- the "k-1"s in Equation (1) look a bit weird 

- First sentence of Section 4 seems broken 

- The arrows in the reactions (e.g. in subscript 2) look weird 

- "transform the feature maps of the teacher and student models in the same shape" - "in" -> "into" 

- "compared with the best-performed MolR model" - "best-performed" -> "best-performing"

Clarity: The work is written very clearly. 

 

Quality: The experiments and comparisons are relatively thorough. 

 

Reproducibility: The appendix provides a lot of hyperparameter and implementation details. Overall, the work looks reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work seems to be a rather small – but useful – update of MolR. The difference between the two approaches is reasonably ablated (although that could be improved, see (W1)). Empirical performance looks good (the margin on top of MolR is not very big, but the model is also smaller). For my initial evaluation, I lean slightly towards acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to use chemical reaction yield data as a source of information in pretraining a model to predict molecular properties. It uses a) a pretraining step where a model is trained with a margin loss to place the reactant and product embeddings of a single reaction at a close point in space and scales the margin by reaction yield to increase focus on high yield reactions b) a knowledge distillation step where a student model is trained to produce similar representations to the original pretrained model, while simultaneously accurately predicting the molecular property. The overall approach hinges on the idea that chemical reaction information can enrich molecular representations for property prediction, and the novelty is that adding in reaction yield improves performance compared to previous approaches. The method is evaluated on a selection of benchmark tasks from MoleculeNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
* The work presents an effective approach to pretraining molecular representations for use in downstream molecular property prediction tasks, making use of the additional information in the yield, which demonstrates gains in data efficiency in pretraining and some overall performance gain on key benchmarks.   

Weaknesses:
* This work is of marginal novelty, given that chemical reactions have been used in pretraining as in the paper which is cited as Wang 2022a.
* The performance gains on the MoleculeNet tasks are, for many of the tasks, are overlapping with other baseline methods within error bars. For instance, on Tox21, performance is overlapping clearly with MolR within standard error, this is true for several other tasks (notably HIV and ClinTox). Therefore, it cannot be claimed that this method clearly beats state of the art. 
* It is unclear why pretraining using molecular reactions with a yield-based margin loss should be effective; yields are of course a function of the reactants but are strongly influenced by the conditions of a reaction and additional reagents. The paper would benefit from discussion around this point, and elaboration or physical explanation as to why yields are a particularly useful pretraining component.  
* In addition, the authors present MolKD- results, focusing only on the reaction-based pretraining. The gains made by full MolKD (indicating the gains of knowledge distillation) are marginal at best over this. This raises the question as to whether the method is really learning any significant task information in the distillation step.
* Did the authors try fine-tuning on molecular property prediction following the pretraining step, rather than using knowledge distillation? It would be helpful to know the value of yield-augmented reaction-driven molecular representations as compared to other pretraining methods such as the self-supervising methods of Hu et al. by comparing the pretrained model as a starting point for fine-tuning, before bringing in a knowledge distillation step. 
* The comparison of structural similarity in Figure 4 is of unclear value. Are the closest molecules in the MolKD representation closer by Tanimoto similarity than the set that would be found from another method eg. MolR? The set of closest molecules currently looks much  like would be found with many pretraining methods. Clarity on how this demonstrates the specific value of the author's approach would be appreciated.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: 
The paper is reasonably clearly written, and the method well presented. 

Novelty:
The work has marginal novelty, primarily limited to the use of yields in pretraining from chemical reactions, and some knowledge distillation. Work cited in the paper has previously used chemical reactions in pretraining and the performance gains over those results are not clear. 

Reproducibility:
Source code is made available in the supplementary material.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work has marginal novelty, primarily limited to the use of yields in pretraining from chemical reactions, and some knowledge distillation. Work cited in the paper has previously used chemical reactions in pretraining.  The knowledge distillation step has a small effect only on performance, and the use of yields is not well-justified. The performance against common baselines is not clearly outperforming the current state of the art in this area, as results are within standard error of current SOTA. It is not currently possible to ascribe performance gains, if they exist, to the additional information leveraged by the model in using yields, and there is not a strong physical or theoretical justification for doing so either.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a framework that incorporates reaction yield in reaction pre-training and distills pre-trained knowledge to assist molecular property prediction. For pre-training, they introduce yield information to adaptively modify the margins between the positive samples and the negative samples. For distillation, they leverage a feature-based distillation method to transfer knowledge to downstream tasks. Experiments are conducted to verify the superiority of the methods on chemical reaction prediction and properties prediction tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The structure of the article is clear.
* MolKD achieves good results across many datasets.
* The idea of uncertainty KG is interesting.

Weaknesses:
* The key motivation of this paper is trivial. This work adds an adaptive yield margin to the MolR method but lacks explanation (see below).
* Knowledge distillation doesn't seem to be necessary. The advantage of using the teacher-student model is not well-explained in the scenario of offline distillation.
* The key results on the property prediction tasks are based on random split rather than scaffold split, which cannot prove the generalization ability of proposed pre-training strategy.

Questions:
* The rationale of using yield as uncertainty needs further elaboration. First, the yield is affected by the experimental conditions and the state of the molecule, etc. Different experimental conditions will lead to completely different results (i.e. uncertainty in this paper). Second, 0.8 and 0.9 are very high yields in organic synthesis. But under the experimental setting of this paper, the coefficients of margin gamma will be 0.64 and 0.81. Does this over-distinguish two reactions? The author should provide some explanations to prove that the contribution of the yield as uncertainty to the experiment is enough to offset the noise and make the hypothesis in this paper more solid.
* The authors use their own dataset to re-train MolR, leading to significant performance degradation. It seems that the MolR model has not been tuned extensively. The tuning process should be provided. Moreover, the requirement of yield data limits MolKD to be trained in a larger dataset, so the comparasion is not that fair to MolR.
* The random split of the property prediction datasets make little sense for pre-training methods. This is because the performance are highly random and cannot prove the generalisation power of pre-training strategies [1][2]. The authors should add some scaffold split or OGB split  (https://ogb.stanford.edu/) results for comparasion. 
* There are some typos in the manuscript, such as “TrasE”. 

[1] Hu et al. Strategies for Pre-training Graph Neural Networks. ICLR 2019
[2] Rong et al. Self-Supervised Graph Transformer on Large-Scale Molecular Data. NeurIPS 2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is overall well-written and easy to follow. The idea is original but not well-motivated. The code for these experiments is provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: In general, I think it is interesting to introduce uncertain knowledge graphs. However, the link between uncertainty and yield lacks explanations. The experimental results cannot support the generalization ability of the proposed model.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Most previous methods of molecular representation learning start from 2D or 3D structures of molecules, and rarely involve specific chemical knowledge. In this paper, the proposed MolKD framework transfers cross-modal knowledge between the pre-training of chemical reaction datasets and the downstream task, e.g., molecular property prediction, by knowledge distillation. MolKD introduces reaction yields during pre-training, which empirically improves the performance in downstream tasks. The authors also conduct some visualization experiments and case studies to describe that MolKD has some robustness and interpretability.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- MolKD distills the knowledge pre-trained on the chemical reaction dataset to the downstream task of property prediction. This approach is novel to some extent.
- The authors introduce reaction yields in the pre-training objective on chemical reaction datasets to help improve downstream task performance.
- The authors conduct some visualizations and case studies to help illustrate the robustness and interpretability of MolKD.
### Weaknesses
- The contribution is not clear, it seems the proposed method is largely based on MolR (Wang et al., 2022a), plus with a knowledge distillation and GTransE (Kertkei-dkachorn et al., 2019). 
- Sec 5.2, Table 2, Tabel 5. The dataset splitting in the molecular property prediction task is not aligned with the baseline. The splitting used in the paper is random splitting, while PretrainGNN, Grover-base, and MolCLR-GCN/GIN, GEM, GraphMVP are not random splitting according to those papers. PretrainGNN, GEM, and GraphMVP are scaffold splitting; MolCLR-GCN/GIN is scaffold splitting without considering molecular chirality; Grover-base is balanced-scaffold splitting. One model usually performs worse in scaffold splitting than random splitting due to the out-of-distribution molecular scaffold. For these baselines, the experimental setup of molecular property prediction in this paper is not the same, and the results are not directly comparable. For the other baselines, it would be nice if the authors could double-check them.
- Sec 4.1, "Preserving chemical reaction equivalence." In the dataset used for the experiments in this paper, the products of chemical reactions ignore by-products (e.g., water).
- Sec 3, "Uncertainty knowledge graphs (KG)." The relation between MolKD described in the paper and uncertainty knowledge graphs (KG) is not clearly described. 
- Typo "TrasE" in Sec 2
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
Quality
- Some experiment results are wrong, referring to "Weaknesses".
Novelty
- It seems the proposed method is largely based on MolR (Wang et al., 2022a).
Reproducibility
- The experimental setup for molecular property prediction is not aligned with baselines.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, due to the novelty and wrong experiment setting, I recommend rejection.

content.title: Distilling Pre-trained Knowledge in Chemical Reactions for Molecular Property Prediction
content.abstract: How to effectively represent molecules is a long-standing challenge for molecular property prediction and drug discovery. Recently, accumulative unlabelled molecule data have spurred the rapid development of pre-training methods for molecular representation learning. However, these works mainly focus on devising self-supervised learning tasks and/or introducing 3D geometric information based on molecular structures with little chemical domain knowledge involved. To address this issue, we propose a novel method (MolKD) by Distilling pre-trained Knowledge in chemical reactions to assist Molecular property prediction. Specifically, MolKD first learns effective representations by incorporating reaction yields to measure transformation efficiency of the reactant-product pair when pre-training on reactions. Next, MolKD introduces the reaction-to-molecule distillation to transfer cross-modal knowledge between pre-training chemical reaction data and the downstream molecular property prediction tasks. Extensive experiments show that our method can learn effective molecular representations, achieving superior performance compared with state-of-the-art baselines, e.g., 2.8% absolute Hit@1 gain on USPTO in chemical reaction prediction and 1.6% absolute AUC-ROC gain on Tox21 with 1/3 pre-training data size in molecular property prediction. Further investigations on pre-trained molecular representations indicate that MolKD learns to distinguish chemically meaningful molecular similarities, which enables molecular property prediction with high robustness and interpretability.
